t-train.overview: Training is how a model's weights get their values, and for modern LLMs it happens in two broad phases. [Pre-training](#c/pretraining) teaches next-token prediction over trillions of tokens. It is the expensive part, where knowledge and raw capability come from. [Post-training](#c/post-training) is a much cheaper sequence of stages (SFT, preference learning, reinforcement learning) that turns the resulting base model into an assistant. It is where behaviour, alignment and, since 2025, most headline reasoning gains are shaped. Around these phases sit decisions about how to spend compute ([Chinchilla scaling](#c/chinchilla)), whether to update every weight or only small adapters ([LoRA](#c/lora)), and whether to train one generalist or [specialists that are later merged](#c/merging). The chat noted a clear shift: recent architecture changes mostly bought efficiency, while the quality gains came from the training recipe, especially scaled-up RL.

t-data.overview: Data covers what goes into a model's training sets and how that raw material is refined. For pre-training, the backbone is a [filtered web crawl](#c/web-crawl): Common Crawl text run through extraction, deduplication and [model-based quality filtering](#c/quality-filter). Aggressive pipelines like DCLM and FineWeb-Edu discard roughly 90% of the crawl. Code, papers, books, Wikipedia and math are then mixed in, and choosing the proportions is a craft of its own. Post-training data is smaller but costs far more per example. It consists of demonstrations ([synthetic SFT responses](#c/synthetic-sft)), preference pairs (increasingly labelled by an LLM judge) and [verifiable problems](#c/verifiable-problems) for RL, all decontaminated against benchmarks. Flagship labs keep their data secret, so most of what is known comes from fully open efforts such as Dolma, FineWeb, DCLM and [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3).

pretraining.overview: Pre-training is the first and most expensive phase of building a language model. A randomly initialised transformer learns to predict the next token over a huge corpus of mostly web text, measured in trillions of tokens (Llama 4 Maverick about 22T, GLM-5 28.5T), using months of accelerator time. The objective is simple: given the tokens so far, assign high probability to the one that actually comes next. Getting good at that forces the model to absorb grammar, facts, code and patterns of reasoning. The output is a **base model**. It has a lot of latent capability but is not yet an assistant, and asked a question it may simply continue with more questions. [Post-training](#c/post-training) then elicits and directs that capability. How pre-training compute is split between parameters and data is governed by [Chinchilla scaling](#c/chinchilla), and the quality of the corpus ([data curation](#c/c-data-lever)) has turned out to be one of the biggest levers.
pretraining.article:
**Pre-training** is the phase in which a language model learns language and world knowledge from scratch by predicting the next token over a vast text corpus. It accounts for the great majority of a model's training compute: trillions of tokens and months of accelerator time. It produces a *base model*, a raw next-token predictor with enormous latent capability but no orientation toward following instructions or holding a conversation. Everything that makes a model feel like an assistant comes afterwards, in [post-training](#c/post-training).

## How it works

The model (for current LLMs, a [decoder-only transformer](#c/transformer)) reads text that has been split into tokens by a tokenizer. At every position it outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next token. The loss is the cross-entropy between that distribution and the token that actually came next. Gradients flow back through every layer and all weights are updated. The same step is repeated across the whole corpus, usually in a single pass or close to it.

The objective is deceptively simple. To predict the next token well across web pages, code, papers and books, a model has to internalise syntax, facts, arithmetic, programming idioms and the structure of arguments. In the chat's phrasing, pre-training *builds the capabilities*, and post-training *elicits and directs them*.

Some typical scales from the chat:

| Model | Parameters (total / active) | Pre-training tokens |
|---|---|---|
| [Llama 4 Maverick](#c/llama4) | 400B / 17B | ~22T |
| [GLM-5](#c/glm-5) | 744B / ~40B | 28.5T |

## The corpus

Pre-training data is dominated by [filtered web crawl](#c/web-crawl) derived from Common Crawl, with curated sources layered on top: code, academic papers, books, Wikipedia, Q&A sites and math. Building it means [extraction and cleaning](#c/extraction), [deduplication](#c/dedup), [model-based quality filtering](#c/quality-filter) and [decontamination](#c/decontamination). The dominant move is throwing data away. The [DCLM](#c/dclm) benchmark showed that better curation alone, with architecture and training held fixed, could beat the previous open-data state of the art by about 6 MMLU points at half the compute.

## Why it matters

Pre-training sets the ceiling. A widely discussed question (see [RLVR](#c/rlvr)) is whether later reinforcement learning can push a model *beyond* what its base model could already do, or mostly sharpens what was learned here. Either way, the base model's knowledge and raw ability come from this phase.

It is also where most of the compute bill has historically gone. Frontier training compute has grown about 5× per year since 2020 (doubling roughly every 5.2 months), and pre-training compute efficiency has improved about 3× per year. How to spend that compute, bigger model or more data, is the question [Chinchilla scaling](#c/chinchilla) answers: roughly 20 tokens per parameter for a compute-optimal run. Its influence helps explain why frontier models shrank after [GPT-4](#c/gpt-4) and put the extra compute into data.

## Trade-offs and variations

- **Compute-optimal vs. inference-optimal.** Chinchilla minimises training cost for a given quality. Labs that will serve a model billions of times often train a smaller model on far more tokens than 20 per parameter, because it is cheaper to run afterwards.
- **Mid-training / continued pre-training.** The boundary with post-training is fuzzy. Labs often run an intermediate stage heavy in math and code, or extend context length (for example with YaRN), before formal post-training begins.
- **Architecture choices** such as [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) change what "model size" means. Total parameters set memorisation capacity, while active parameters set the per-token cost.
- **Secrecy.** Even open-weight models almost never release their pre-training data, partly for competitive reasons and increasingly for legal ones (copyright and consent scrutiny).

## From the chat

- Pre-training was described as "the expensive, compute-heavy phase": trillions of tokens and months of GPU time, producing a base model that "has read the entire internet but has never been told what they're supposed to *do* with that."
- The chat attributed the post-GPT-4 shrinkage of frontier models partly to Chinchilla: capability that would have come from more parameters came from more and better data on a smaller model.
- On corpora, the chat's headline was "aggressive throwing-away". DCLM and FineWeb-Edu discard the lowest-quality ~90%, and DCLM-Baseline let a 7B model reach 64% MMLU on only 2.6T tokens.
- The chat declined to give a percentage for how much research effort goes into data. It said data work "plausibly rivals or exceeds" architecture and training-code work, and called any specific "X%" figure folklore.
- Flagship recipes remain hidden. Nearly everything concrete about pre-training data comes from open-data projects, and whether closed labs do the same is inference.

sft.overview: Supervised fine-tuning is the first stage of [post-training](#c/post-training). The model keeps doing exactly what it did in pre-training, predicting the next token, but now on a curated dataset of prompts paired with ideal responses: thousands to millions of "here's a question, here's a good answer" demonstrations. This teaches the *format* of being an assistant, meaning that questions get answers, instructions get followed and conversations take turns. It does most of the work of turning a base model into something that behaves like a helper. Its limit is that the model can only imitate what it is shown, and good demonstrations are expensive to write. Increasingly they are [generated by stronger models](#c/synthetic-sft). Tülu 3's new SFT responses came from GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet, which makes SFT the main channel for [distillation](#c/distillation). Later stages ([reward modeling](#c/reward-model), RL) build on the SFT model.
sft.article:
**Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)**, also called *instruction tuning*, is the first stage of [post-training](#c/post-training). It keeps the same learning mechanism as [pre-training](#c/pretraining), next-token prediction with a cross-entropy loss, but swaps the raw web corpus for a curated dataset of *examples of the behaviour you want*: prompts paired with high-quality responses. It is the step that makes a base model act like an assistant at all.

## How it works

Each training example is a prompt (possibly a multi-turn conversation) plus a target response, formatted with the chat template the model will use at inference. The loss is usually computed only on the response tokens, so the model learns to *produce* good answers rather than to predict the user's words. Training runs for relatively few steps, at a learning rate well below pre-training's, so the model's knowledge is redirected rather than overwritten.

What the model learns is mostly behavioural:

- that a question should be followed by a helpful answer rather than by more questions;
- that instructions and format constraints should be obeyed;
- the turn-taking structure of a conversation;
- style, tone, and the refusal patterns written into the demonstrations.

SFT can be done as full fine-tuning or with [LoRA](#c/lora). LoRA is extremely common for SFT specifically, especially outside the frontier labs.

## Where the data comes from

Datasets range from thousands to about a million examples. [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3)'s SFT mixture has 939,344 samples drawn from many sources, including FLAN v2, CoCoNot and WildChat. Prompts come from three buckets: paid annotators, real user logs, and model-synthesized prompts (for example persona-driven generation for diversity). Responses are increasingly [synthetic](#c/synthetic-sft). All of Tülu 3's *new* SFT responses were written by GPT-4o, or by Claude 3.5 Sonnet for coding, because those gave the best results. Regenerating completions for existing datasets through that pipeline even improved downstream [DPO](#c/dpo) performance. Everything is [decontaminated](#c/decontamination) against evaluation benchmarks.

Closed frontier labs cannot do this for their flagship models, because there is no stronger model to copy. They rely more on paid human experts and on their own earlier models.

## SFT as distillation

Training on a stronger model's outputs is output-based [distillation](#c/distillation). It is the only form available when the teacher is a closed API, since you cannot see its weights or probabilities. Much of the 2023–2024 open-model wave (Alpaca, which fine-tuned Llama on about 52K model-generated instructions; Open Orca; ShareGPT-trained models) was SFT-as-distillation. TinyGSM showed how strong the effect can be: 12.3M synthetic math problems from GPT-3.5-turbo got a 125M-parameter model to 63.1% on grade-school math. DeepSeek likewise distilled [DeepSeek-R1](#c/deepseek-r1)'s reasoning into smaller models via SFT on its traces.

## Limitations

- **Imitation ceiling.** The model can only be as good as its demonstrations. It never sees what a *better* answer would look like.
- **Cost and coverage.** High-quality human demonstrations are expensive and cannot cover every situation.
- **Forgetting.** Push too hard (high learning rate, too many steps) and fluency or knowledge degrade.

These limits motivate the next stages. [Reward modeling](#c/reward-model) turns cheaper *comparisons* into a training signal, and reinforcement learning ([RLHF](#c/rlhf), [RLVR](#c/rlvr)) lets the model explore and be rewarded for outputs better than any in the SFT set.

## In practice

Real pipelines rarely run SFT once. Labs interleave SFT and RL over several rounds, and they often run an SFT "cold start" on curated reasoning traces before large-scale RL. For someone adapting an open model to a domain, SFT with LoRA is the default and often the only step.

## From the chat

- The chat called SFT the stage that "does most of the heavy lifting in converting a base model into something that behaves like an assistant at all". The mechanism is the same as pre-training, and only the data differs.
- It named SFT's core limitation: the model "can only imitate the demonstrations it's shown", which is why RL can in principle exceed it.
- It called distillation "essentially a souped-up SFT," and noted that for the instruction-following quality of 2023–2024 open models, "a great deal of it, openly" came from frontier outputs.
- It highlighted the Tülu 3 admission that its synthetic SFT responses were written by GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet. This is where the open recipe and the frontier recipe genuinely diverge.

reward-model.overview: Reward modeling rests on a simple observation: it is much easier to say which of two answers is better than to write the ideal answer yourself. So after [SFT](#c/sft), labs collect *comparison* data. Humans, or increasingly [an LLM judge](#c/llm-judge), see two responses to the same prompt and pick the preferred one. A separate network, usually initialised from the SFT model with a scalar output head, is trained to give the preferred response a higher score. Once trained, it can score any new response, and that turns fuzzy human taste into a number [RLHF](#c/rlhf) can optimise. It is also RLHF's weak point. A learned reward model is a noisy, gameable proxy, and a policy optimised hard against it can learn to please the scorer without actually being better. [DPO](#c/dpo) avoids training one at all, and [RLVR](#c/rlvr) swaps it for a deterministic checker where correctness can be verified.
reward-model.article:
**Reward modeling** is the [post-training](#c/post-training) stage that turns *preferences* into a trainable signal. Instead of showing the model ideal answers, as [SFT](#c/sft) does, you show a judge pairs of answers and record which one is better, then train a **reward model** to predict those judgments. The reward model then acts as an automated critic that can score any response. It supplies the "human feedback" in [RLHF](#c/rlhf).

## Why comparisons

The motivating insight is asymmetric difficulty. Writing a perfect response to a hard prompt is slow and expensive, while comparing two candidate responses is fast and needs less expertise. Comparisons also capture qualities that are hard to demonstrate but easy to recognise: tone, helpfulness, appropriate caution, concision. Because they rank the model's *own* outputs, they tell it about the region of behaviour it actually occupies.

## How it works

1. **Collect prompts** and sample several responses per prompt, from the model being trained and often from a pool of other models.
2. **Label preferences.** An annotator marks which response is preferred, producing (prompt, chosen, rejected) triples. Classic RLHF used human annotators. Open pipelines such as [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3) now lean heavily on [LLM-as-a-judge](#c/llm-judge), and Qwen2 describes a human–automation hybrid.
3. **Train the reward model.** Typically this is a copy of the SFT model with its output head replaced by a single scalar. The standard objective (a Bradley–Terry-style pairwise loss) pushes the chosen response's score above the rejected one's.
4. **Use it.** The reward model scores fresh generations during reinforcement learning, or filters and ranks samples.

Post-training data therefore has two main ingredients, demonstrations for SFT and preference pairs for this stage. For the 8B Tülu 3 model the preference set was roughly 250–300K pairs.

## Trade-offs and failure modes

- **Proxy, not truth.** The reward model only approximates what the labellers wanted. The chat called it "a noisy, gameable proxy": a policy optimised against it can learn to satisfy the reward model without being right. This is *reward hacking*, and it is why RLHF usually adds a penalty for drifting too far from the SFT model.
- **Label noise and bias.** Humans disagree and have systematic tastes (for example, preferring longer answers). LLM judges bring biases of their own.
- **Coverage.** A reward model is only reliable near the distribution it was trained on. As the policy improves, its outputs can drift out of that region.
- **Extra machinery.** A separate network has to be trained, stored and run during RL.

## Alternatives and successors

- **[DPO](#c/dpo)** skips the explicit reward model and optimises the policy directly on preference pairs.
- **[RLVR](#c/rlvr)** replaces the learned model with a deterministic verifier (unit tests, answer checking) wherever correctness is objective, which removes the proxy problem in those domains.
- **Process rewards and rubric-based rewards** are active research directions for extending verifier-like signals to domains without ground truth, such as scoring intermediate reasoning steps rather than only final answers.

## In practice

Preference-data construction is empirical and expensive. Tülu 3's ablations found that including on-policy responses (from the model being trained) helped, that scaling the number of unique prompts helped, and that using new prompts rather than reusing SFT prompts helped. How much human judgment remains in frontier labs' preference data is not disclosed.

## From the chat

- The chat described reward modeling as moving from "imitate good examples" to "learn what's *better*," motivated by comparing being easier than writing.
- It stressed that preferences can train a separate reward model or be "used more directly". The latter is the DPO route.
- It called the learned reward model's weakness central to why [RLVR](#c/rlvr) mattered: "a learned reward model is a noisy, gameable proxy … A verifier isn't a proxy; it checks ground truth."
- It flagged the shift toward LLM judges as real but not total, and said the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge is now "load-bearing for the whole preference-data pipeline."

rlhf.overview: RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) is the post-training method that made chat assistants work, and it was popularised by OpenAI's InstructGPT and ChatGPT around 2022. It builds on [SFT](#c/sft) and a trained [reward model](#c/reward-model) that scores responses the way human raters would. The model then generates responses, the reward model scores them, and a reinforcement-learning algorithm (classically PPO, with a separate critic network) updates the model toward higher-scoring outputs. A penalty keeps it from drifting too far from the SFT model. Unlike imitation, RL lets the model be rewarded for answers better than any demonstration. Its weakness is that the reward is a learned, gameable proxy. That led to two successors: [DPO](#c/dpo), which skips the reward model, and [RLVR](#c/rlvr), which replaces it with a checker for math and code.
rlhf.article:
**Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)** is a [post-training](#c/post-training) technique that optimises a language model against a learned model of human preferences. It was the method that turned instruction-tuned models into the helpful, conversational assistants of 2022 onward, with OpenAI's InstructGPT and ChatGPT the best-known examples. It remains the standard way to shape subjective qualities like helpfulness, tone and harmlessness.

## How it works

RLHF sits at stage 3 of the classic pipeline:

1. **[SFT](#c/sft)** gives a model that already behaves roughly like an assistant.
2. **[Reward modeling](#c/reward-model).** Humans compare pairs of responses, and a reward model is trained to predict which one they prefer.
3. **RL optimisation.** The SFT model (now the *policy*) generates responses to prompts. The reward model scores each one, and a policy-gradient algorithm updates the policy to make high-scoring responses more likely.

The classic algorithm is **PPO** (Proximal Policy Optimization). PPO uses a separate *critic* or value network to estimate how good each step is, and it clips updates to keep training stable. Two further ingredients are standard:

- a **KL penalty** against the frozen SFT (reference) model, so the policy cannot drift into strange text that happens to score well;
- the **reward model itself**, kept frozen during RL.

During training that is up to four models in memory: policy, reference, reward model and critic. This is part of why RLHF is expensive and fiddly.

## Why it matters

RL goes beyond imitation. SFT can only copy its demonstrations, but RL lets the model explore its own outputs and be rewarded for ones better than anything in the demonstration set. So RLHF can in principle exceed the quality of the human-written examples. It is also where much fine-grained behaviour gets shaped: tone, helpfulness, refusals, harmlessness. The chat noted that safety and alignment behaviour lives predominantly in post-training.

## Trade-offs and failure modes

- **Reward hacking.** The reward model is a learned proxy, and optimising hard against it finds its blind spots, such as responses that *look* good to the scorer without being correct. The KL penalty mitigates this but does not remove it.
- **Cost.** The critic roughly doubles memory and compute relative to the policy alone, and the whole setup has many hyperparameters.
- **Subjective signal.** Human preference is well suited to style and helpfulness but a poor signal for correctness in math or code, where raters may not be able to tell.

## What it led to

Two lines of work each removed a piece of RLHF:

| Successor | What it removes | Idea |
|---|---|---|
| [DPO](#c/dpo) (2023) | The separate reward model and RL loop | Optimise the policy directly on preference pairs |
| [RLVR](#c/rlvr) (2025) | The *learned* reward | Use a deterministic checker where correctness is objective |
| [GRPO](#c/grpo) (2024) | The critic network | Use a group of samples' average reward as the baseline |

For reasoning models, RLVR with GRPO has become the dominant stage-3 technique. RLHF-style preference optimisation remains the tool for open-ended qualities where no verifier exists.

## From the chat

- The chat placed RLHF and RLVR as "both *Stage 3* techniques" that "differ in where the reward comes from". RLHF's learned reward is "good for subjective qualities like helpfulness and tone, but a noisy, gameable proxy."
- It explained that PPO "needs a separate 'critic' or value network … that roughly doubles the memory and compute". Removing that critic is GRPO's main contribution.
- It presented DPO as RLHF's "known alternative", simpler and popular in open models, and said whether it matches full RL at scale is debated.
- It noted the shift from human raters to [LLM judges](#c/llm-judge) in open pipelines, which means that for many open models the "human" in RLHF is increasingly a model.

dpo.overview: DPO (Direct Preference Optimization, 2023) gets most of the benefit of [RLHF](#c/rlhf) without training a separate [reward model](#c/reward-model) or running a reinforcement-learning loop. Its key result is mathematical. The optimal policy under RLHF's KL-regularised objective can be written in closed form, so the reward is *implied* by the policy itself. That allows training directly on (prompt, chosen, rejected) triples with a simple classification-style loss. The loss raises the model's likelihood of the chosen response relative to a frozen reference model, and lowers it for the rejected one. No sampling happens during training and no critic is needed, so DPO is cheap, stable and easy to run. It became very popular in open models, for example in the [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3) recipe. Whether it matches full online RL at frontier scale is debated.
dpo.article:
**Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)** is a [post-training](#c/post-training) method, introduced in 2023, that aligns a model to preference data without an explicit [reward model](#c/reward-model) or a reinforcement-learning loop. It combines stages 2 and 3 of the classic [RLHF](#c/rlhf) pipeline into one supervised-style training step. That makes it much simpler to run, and it has become a staple of open-model post-training.

## How it works

RLHF optimises a policy to maximise a learned reward while a KL penalty keeps it close to a reference model, usually the [SFT](#c/sft) model. DPO's authors showed that this objective has a closed-form optimal solution. The reward can be written in terms of the ratio between the policy's probability of a response and the reference model's. Substituting that back into the standard pairwise preference loss leaves a loss that depends only on the policy and the reference, so no separate reward network is needed.

In practice, for each (prompt, chosen, rejected) triple:

1. compute how much more likely the chosen response is under the policy than under the frozen reference;
2. compute the same for the rejected response;
3. push the first up relative to the second, through a logistic loss scaled by a temperature β that sets how far the policy may move from the reference.

That is the whole procedure. There is no generation during training, no critic, and no reward model to train or keep in memory.

## Why it matters

- **Simplicity and cost.** Two models (policy and frozen reference) instead of RLHF's four, and a training loop that looks like fine-tuning.
- **Stability.** Fewer moving parts and hyperparameters than PPO-based RLHF.
- **Accessibility.** A team that can do SFT can do DPO, often with [LoRA](#c/lora). That largely explains its spread through open models.

The chat described it as "a lighter-weight Stage 2+3 combined," "simpler and popular in open models."

## Trade-offs

- **Offline data.** Standard DPO learns from a fixed set of preference pairs rather than sampling fresh outputs and scoring them. If those pairs come from other models, the signal may not match the policy's own mistakes. [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3)'s ablations found that including *on-policy* responses (from the model being trained) in the preference data improved results.
- **Bounded by the preferences.** Like RLHF it inherits the biases of whoever labelled the pairs, increasingly an [LLM judge](#c/llm-judge).
- **Not for verifiable reasoning.** For math and code, where correctness can be checked, online RL with a verifier ([RLVR](#c/rlvr)) has become the dominant approach for reasoning models.
- **Scale question.** Whether DPO matches full online RL at the frontier is openly debated. Frontier labs' exact recipes are undisclosed.

## In practice

A common open recipe is SFT, then DPO on preference pairs, then (for reasoning) RLVR on [verifiable problems](#c/verifiable-problems). That is the shape of Tülu 3, which found that regenerating SFT completions through its synthetic pipeline improved DPO performance, and that scaling unique prompts and using prompts not seen in SFT helped. Many variants that tweak the loss have followed, but the basic method remains the default.

## From the chat

- The chat introduced DPO as RLHF's "known alternative" that "skips training a separate reward model and optimizes the model directly on preference pairs."
- It said DPO is "simpler and popular in open models," and that "whether it matches full RL at scale is debated". This is presented as an open question, not a settled one.
- The Tülu 3 findings (on-policy data, more unique prompts, new prompts rather than reused SFT prompts) were cited as examples of how much ablation building good preference data takes.

rlvr.overview: RLVR (reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards) replaces [RLHF](#c/rlhf)'s learned [reward model](#c/reward-model) with a deterministic checker. It runs the code against unit tests, compares the math answer with ground truth, or checks a format constraint, and gives a binary pass/fail reward. Because the checker verifies correctness itself, there is no noisy proxy for the model to game. That makes it especially effective in math and code, and it has become the dominant post-training paradigm for reasoning models. [DeepSeek-R1](#c/deepseek-r1) was the landmark case: RL on correct answers alone produced long chains of thought and a spontaneous "aha moment" of self-reflection. [GRPO](#c/grpo) made it affordable. Two questions remain open: how to extend it to domains with no verifier, and whether it [creates new reasoning or mainly sharpens](#c/c-rlvr-new) what the base model could already do.
rlvr.article:
**Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR)** is a [post-training](#c/post-training) method in which a model is optimised against a *deterministic verifier* rather than a learned judge. The model attempts a problem, a program checks whether the result is correct, and the model is reinforced toward attempts that pass. Since early 2025 it has become the dominant technique for training reasoning models, and it underlies much of the test-time-compute paradigm, in which models "think" at length before answering.

## How it works

RLVR is a stage-3 (reinforcement learning) technique, like [RLHF](#c/rlhf). What changes is where the reward comes from:

| | RLHF | RLVR |
|---|---|---|
| Reward source | Learned [reward model](#c/reward-model) of human preference | Rule-based checker |
| Signal | Continuous score, noisy | Usually binary: correct or not |
| Gameable? | Yes, it is a proxy | Much less, since it checks ground truth |
| Best domains | Tone, helpfulness, style | Math, code, checkable constraints |

A typical loop samples a batch of [verifiable problems](#c/verifiable-problems), generates several reasoning traces per problem, scores each final answer with the verifier, and updates the policy. The standard update algorithm is [GRPO](#c/grpo), which compares each attempt with the group's average and so needs no critic network. That cost saving is a large part of why reasoning training spread so quickly across labs.

## Why it matters

The striking result came from [DeepSeek-R1](#c/deepseek-r1). Optimising only for correct final answers made the model *learn to reason at length*. Extended chain-of-thought, self-reflection ("wait, let me reconsider") and branching emerged during training without being taught, which researchers called an "aha moment." RLVR teaches a model to *use* inference-time thinking productively.

It also drove visible capability jumps. [DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/deepseek-v32)'s rise to GPT-5-comparable performance came from "a scalable RL framework and scaled-up post-training compute," and its Speciale variant reached gold-medal level at the 2025 IMO and IOI. Competition math and coding are the showcases because they are the most verifiable domains.

## Failure modes

- **Length bias.** Naive RLVR tends to make reasoning chains ever longer, sometimes without improving them.
- **Exploration collapse.** If every sampled attempt at a problem is wrong, the group has no variation and there is no learning signal. This is severe on hard or unfamiliar problems.
- **Reward hacking.** The model may find ways to satisfy the checker without genuine reasoning (for example, exploiting weak tests), so reward design matters.

The [GRPO variants](#c/grpo-variants) (DAPO, Dr. GRPO, VAPO and others) are mostly patches for these problems. Data work matters too: curated verifiable datasets balanced toward medium difficulty, [decontaminated](#c/decontamination) against benchmarks, often with curricula of increasing difficulty.

## The contested question

Does RLVR create genuinely new reasoning ability? A careful [coverage study](#c/rlvr-study) found that across PPO, GRPO and others, RLVR *increases the likelihood* of correct samples but *decreases coverage* of solvable problems. The model gets better at sampling answers it could already produce, but gains no capability beyond the base model. The same work found that [distillation](#c/distillation) *can* transfer new reasoning patterns, and that current RLVR algorithms perform similarly and "remain far from optimal." Other work reports broader gains. The chat treated this as "a serious, credible critique rather than settled fact," with the truth depending on what counts as "new." See [the claim](#c/c-rlvr-new).

## The open frontier

The hard problem is **extending verifiable rewards beyond cleanly checkable domains**, such as essays, legal analysis, or agents over 50 tool calls. Candidate approaches include learned verifiers, rubric-based rewards and process rewards that score intermediate steps. Agentic RL, training models to use tools over long horizons, is probably the biggest current frontier. Frontier labs' exact RL recipes are undisclosed.

## From the chat

- The chat called RLVR "the dominant post-training paradigm for reasoning models" and a "clean departure" from RLHF. It swaps a noisy, gameable proxy for a verifier that "checks ground truth."
- It described R1's "aha moment" as the landmark demonstration: self-reflection "fell out of optimizing for correct answers over long reasoning chains."
- It gave real weight to the finding that RLVR sharpens rather than expands ability, but labelled it one research line, not consensus. It also noted that the alphabet of variants "may matter less than the marketing implies."
- It named extension to soft domains as the unresolved problem, and agentic RL as the area where its knowledge was least current.

grpo.overview: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is the reinforcement-learning algorithm that made [RLVR](#c/rlvr) cheap enough to spread across labs. It was introduced in DeepSeek's 2024 math work and used for [DeepSeek-R1](#c/deepseek-r1). Standard PPO, the RLHF workhorse, runs a separate critic or value network next to the model to estimate how good each step is, which roughly doubles memory and compute. GRPO drops the critic. For each problem it samples a *group* of attempts (say 16) and scores them all, for example with a verifier. Each attempt's advantage is its reward relative to the group average, normalised by the group's spread. Above-average attempts are reinforced and below-average ones suppressed. The baseline therefore comes from the samples themselves. GRPO became the de facto RLVR algorithm, and its known failure modes spawned [a family of variants](#c/grpo-variants).
grpo.article:
**Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)** is a policy-gradient reinforcement-learning algorithm for language models. It removes the separate critic network that PPO requires and estimates the baseline from a group of sampled responses instead. DeepSeek introduced it in its 2024 math-reasoning work, and it became the de facto algorithm for [RLVR](#c/rlvr) after [DeepSeek-R1](#c/deepseek-r1) used it to train reasoning from scratch.

## Background: the critic problem

Policy-gradient methods need a *baseline*, an estimate of how good an outcome was expected to be, so they can tell whether a particular result was better or worse than usual. PPO, the standard algorithm in [RLHF](#c/rlhf), learns this baseline with a **critic** (value network), usually about as large as the policy. It must be trained alongside the policy, held in memory and run on every step. For large models that roughly doubles the memory and compute of RL training. Learning an accurate per-token value for long reasoning chains is also hard.

## How it works

1. Take a prompt, for example a math problem.
2. Sample a **group** of G responses from the current policy (the chat's example uses 16).
3. Score each response. In RLVR this is a verifier, so typically 1 for correct and 0 for wrong.
4. Compute each response's **advantage** as its reward minus the group mean, divided by the group standard deviation.
5. Update the policy with a PPO-style clipped objective using those advantages, with a KL penalty toward a reference model.

The effect: better-than-average attempts become more likely, and worse-than-average ones less likely. The group *is* the baseline, and no critic is trained.

## Why it matters

- **Cost.** The chat said that removing the critic "leads to a substantial reduction in RL training overhead," and that this is "much of why reasoning training proliferated so fast across labs." GRPO made RLVR affordable.
- **Fit with verifiable rewards.** Binary pass/fail rewards on one problem compare naturally within a group: which attempts got it right?
- **Simplicity.** It needs fewer models in memory and less value-function tuning.

## Failure modes

GRPO's design creates specific problems, and each became the target of a variant (see [GRPO variants](#c/grpo-variants)):

- **Exploration collapse / zero gradient.** If all G attempts fail, or all succeed, every advantage is zero and the problem contributes no learning signal. On hard problems this can stall learning entirely.
- **Length bias.** How the loss is normalised across tokens and sequences can reward long wrong answers or short right ones unevenly. Naive training tends to inflate response length.
- **Per-prompt normalisation bias.** Dividing by each group's standard deviation weights prompts unevenly. REINFORCE++ uses global advantage normalisation instead.
- **MoE instability.** Token-level importance ratios can be unstable for [Mixture-of-Experts](#c/moe) models. GSPO moves optimisation to the sequence level to fix this.

## In practice

GRPO and its descendants are the standard RL algorithms in open reasoning-model reports. Frontier labs do not disclose which algorithms they use. The [coverage study](#c/rlvr-study) cited in the chat found that current RLVR algorithms, PPO and GRPO included, perform similarly to one another and remain far from optimal. That suggests the choice among them may matter less than the data, the verifier and the compute budget.

## From the chat

- The chat called GRPO "the algorithm doing the work": "for one problem, generate (say) 16 attempts, score them all with the verifier, and judge each attempt *relative to the group average*."
- It said GRPO's importance "is mostly about cost". PPO's critic "roughly doubles the memory and compute," and removing it made RLVR affordable.
- It placed GRPO in the same "one breakthrough, then a dense flurry of incremental fixes" pattern the chat saw in architecture, and suggested the variants may matter less than the marketing implies.

grpo-variants.overview: After [GRPO](#c/grpo) became the default algorithm for [RLVR](#c/rlvr), a series of variants appeared, each patching a specific failure mode. DAPO, Dr. GRPO, VC-PPO and VAPO target **length bias**, where naive RL makes reasoning chains ever longer without making them better, as well as difficulty imbalance, value-function management over long chains, and training stability. Several also address **exploration collapse**: when every attempt in a group fails, the group-relative advantage is zero and nothing is learned. Fixes include dynamic sampling, entropy bonuses and curricula. REINFORCE++ swaps GRPO's per-prompt advantage normalisation for a global one to remove a bias. GSPO moves optimisation from the token to the sequence level to stabilise RL on [Mixture-of-Experts](#c/moe) models. The chat's caution: one careful study found current RLVR algorithms perform similarly and remain far from optimal, so the variants may matter less than their marketing implies.

lora.overview: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation, 2021) is the dominant way to fine-tune a model cheaply. It freezes every original weight and trains small "adapter" matrices alongside them. It relies on an empirical regularity: the *change* a model needs during fine-tuning is approximately low-rank. So rather than learning a full 7168×7168 update, it learns two skinny matrices, 7168×16 and 16×7168, whose product approximates it. That is orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters. The payoffs are large. Optimizer state and gradients exist only for the adapter, so fine-tuning fits on one GPU. Because the base is frozen, it cannot be damaged. Adapters are megabytes, so many can be swapped over one base or served together. [QLoRA](#c/qlora) adds a 4-bit base. LoRA dominates [post-training](#c/post-training) of open models outside the frontier labs, while large-scale [RL](#c/rlvr) at the frontier generally uses full fine-tuning.
lora.article:
**LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)** is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method, introduced in 2021. It adapts a pre-trained model by freezing all of its original weights and learning small low-rank update matrices next to selected layers. It has become the default way for companies and individuals to fine-tune open models. As the chat put it, if you have heard of someone "fine-tuning an open model," they almost certainly used LoRA.

## How it works

A transformer layer contains large weight matrices, for example the attention projections and the [feed-forward](#c/ffn) weights. Full fine-tuning updates each of these, W, by some ΔW of the same size. LoRA instead constrains the update to be low-rank:

- **ΔW ≈ B · A**, where A has shape r × d and B has shape d × r, with a small rank *r* (often 8–64).
- For a 7168 × 7168 matrix and r = 16, that means training about 230K numbers instead of about 51M.
- W stays **frozen**, and only A and B receive gradients. B is usually initialised to zero, so training starts exactly at the base model.
- At inference the layer computes W·x + B·A·x. The adapter's contribution can also be merged into W, so there is no extra latency.

The underlying bet is the empirical observation that fine-tuning updates have low "intrinsic rank". This holds well for many adaptation tasks, but it is not a universal law.

## Why it matters

| Benefit | Why |
|---|---|
| Memory and compute | Gradients and optimizer state exist only for the tiny adapter, so large models can be fine-tuned on a single GPU |
| No forgetting by construction | The original weights cannot change, so base capability cannot be damaged |
| Modularity | Adapters are megabytes. You can keep many task-specific ones, swap them over one frozen base, or serve many at once |
| Accessibility | Fine-tuning moves from cluster-scale to workstation-scale |

It also opens modular designs, such as mixtures of cluster-conditional LoRA experts that route different inputs to different adapters. That keeps specialists *inside* one model (see [specialize, then merge](#c/merging)).

## Trade-offs

- **Expressiveness.** Constraining the update to low rank can leave capability on the table. For the deepest behaviour changes, full fine-tuning still tends to win, though the gap has narrowed a lot.
- **Task-dependence.** How much LoRA loses relative to full fine-tuning varies by task and is still being studied.
- **Frontier RL.** Frontier labs are generally understood to do large-scale RL ([RLVR](#c/rlvr)) with full fine-tuning, because they want every parameter available. Their exact recipes are proprietary.

## Full fine-tuning vs. LoRA

The chat separated two axes, *how many* parameters move and *how much*. Full fine-tuning lets every parameter move but gently, with a learning rate often an order of magnitude or more below pre-training's and far fewer tokens. LoRA touches only a small added subset. Both aim to shape behaviour without destroying what [pre-training](#c/pretraining) built.

## Variants

- **[QLoRA](#c/qlora)** quantises the frozen base to 4-bit while keeping adapters at higher precision, which pushes fine-tuning of large models onto consumer hardware.
- Other PEFT methods (adapter layers, prefix tuning) exist, but LoRA and QLoRA dominate in practice.

## In practice

[SFT](#c/sft) with LoRA is extremely common. It is often the entire post-training step for a domain-specific deployment. LoRA also pairs naturally with [DPO](#c/dpo). One complication: for [Mixture-of-Experts](#c/moe) models, updating a sparse, routed model raises extra questions about which experts' parameters move and how routing interacts with the updates.

## From the chat

- The chat called LoRA "the dominant method" of PEFT and described its idea as elegant: freeze the model and train "two skinny matrices like 7168×16 and 16×7168" whose product approximates the update.
- It listed three payoffs: memory and compute, "no forgetting by construction," and modularity.
- It split usage by who is training. Frontier labs do serious behaviour-shaping, especially RL, with full fine-tuning, and "everyone else adapting an existing open model" overwhelmingly uses LoRA.
- It cautioned that the low-rank premise is "an empirical regularity … not a universal law," and that the line between where LoRA suffices and where full fine-tuning wins is "fuzzy and task-dependent."

qlora.overview: QLoRA (2023) is [LoRA](#c/lora) applied on top of a base model quantised to 4-bit precision. The frozen base weights are stored in a compact 4-bit format (the paper introduced a "NormalFloat" data type designed for normally distributed weights) and dequantised on the fly during computation. The small trainable adapters stay at higher precision, so gradients flow through the quantised model into the adapters without losing much accuracy. Since the base model dominates memory, cutting it to roughly a quarter of 16-bit size is what lets large models be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and moderately sized ones on consumer hardware. The original paper also used double quantisation and paged optimizer states to fit into tight memory. The chat described QLoRA as quantising the frozen base "to shrink memory even further". Together with LoRA, it dominates how open models are fine-tuned outside the frontier labs. See also [weight quantization](#c/quantization).

merging.overview: "Specialize, then merge" addresses a real tension in [post-training](#c/post-training). Training one model on many domains brings **positive transfer** (math helps code, and data-rich tasks carry data-poor ones) but also **task interference**, where progress on one skill degrades another. The recipe is to train several specialist models that share a common core of data but differ in their domain-specific portions, then combine them into a single model by **averaging their weights** in chosen proportions. Weight averaging works because models fine-tuned from the same base stay in a compatible region of weight space. That is not obvious, and it only holds within that setting. The result keeps one deployable model while recovering much of what specialists gain. The chat cited an open reasoning model (Apriel) that did exactly this. It [supports the idea](#c/c-specialists) that specialists beat a generalist on their own turf, and shows labs trying to get both.
merging.article:
**Specialize, then merge** is a [post-training](#c/post-training) strategy in which separate specialist models are trained for different domains and then combined into one model by averaging their weights. It is a practical answer to the tension between **task interference** and **positive transfer** in multi-task fine-tuning. It tries to capture a specialist's focus without giving up the deployment simplicity of a single generalist.

## The problem it solves

Your post-training dataset has to serve coders, analysts, writers and more. Two opposite forces act on a single model trained on all of it:

- **Negative transfer / task interference.** Learning one task hinders another, especially when the tasks conflict. Progress on one can oscillate or regress while another improves. A [vision-language study](#c/vl-study) found that on 5 of 7 downstream tasks, a model instruction-tuned on all the data lost to a task expert fine-tuned on just the relevant subset. An expert-LM paper reported +10.4% mean accuracy from selecting relevant experts over a multi-task baseline.
- **Positive transfer.** Diverse [SFT](#c/sft) and RL training builds more fundamental capability, and data-rich tasks regularise data-poor ones. One reasoning-model report found that training on math improved coding, the kind of cross-domain transfer [RLVR](#c/rlvr) pipelines rely on.

Transfer is also **asymmetric**. One late-2025 study found coding and math to be "safe donors" with limited side effects, while factuality and fairness were "intrusive donors" that helped themselves but hurt others. As recipients, coding was receptive and math was brittle. (That is one study's result, not established law.)

## How it works

1. Start from a shared base, typically the same pre-trained or SFT checkpoint.
2. Train several **specialists**. Each sees a common core of data plus a domain-specific portion (math, code, chat, and so on).
3. **Merge** by averaging the specialists' weights parameter by parameter, in chosen proportions, to produce one model.

Weight averaging working at all is non-obvious. It depends on the models sharing an origin: fine-tunes of the same base tend to stay in a connected, low-loss region of weight space, so a weighted average of them is also a good model. Averaging independently trained models generally fails. Research on model merging (model soups, task arithmetic and later interference-aware methods) refines how to combine the differences each fine-tune made, but the core idea is still the average.

## Alternatives

Labs have several ways to get positive transfer while suppressing interference:

| Technique | Idea |
|---|---|
| Data mixing and weighting | One model, with carefully tuned mixture proportions and caps so rare tasks don't dominate |
| Sequential / staged training | Order tasks, group compatible ones, and use replay or [distillation](#c/distillation) to prevent forgetting |
| Specialize, then merge | Separate training, one combined model |
| Modular routing | Different parameters per task inside one model, e.g. mixtures of [LoRA](#c/lora) experts, an idea related to [MoE](#c/moe) |

## Trade-offs

- A merged model may not match each specialist on its own domain, because averaging dilutes some of each.
- Choosing the proportions is empirical and needs evaluation across all domains.
- Scale matters. Most specialist-beats-generalist evidence comes from SFT and smaller or vision-language settings. Very large models seem to absorb diverse tasks with *less* interference, so the benefit may shrink at frontier scale.

## In practice

The open reasoning-model report the chat cited, Apriel, balanced negative interference against positive transfer by training specialized models on a shared core with varying domain-specific data, then averaging their weights in specified proportions. Whether frontier labs specialize and merge, route, or simply mix is proprietary. The open evidence suggests they grapple with the same tension.

## From the chat

- The user's intuition, that different domains want different post-training, was called "a real and actively studied hypothesis" under the names task interference and negative transfer.
- It is cited as the main mechanism behind the claim that [specialists beat a generalist on their own turf](#c/c-specialists) in practice, since labs specialize, then merge.
- The chat called specialize-then-merge "the hybrid that most directly vindicates your intuition while keeping a single deployable model."
- It stressed that both positive transfer and interference are real, that their balance depends on task relatedness, and that good pipelines are built to exploit the first and suppress the second.
- It cautioned that the specialist advantage may be weaker at frontier scale, and that labs' actual choices (separate RL per domain, mixture weights, merge or route) are unknown.

chinchilla.overview: Chinchilla scaling is DeepMind's 2022 finding about how to spend a fixed training-compute budget. The field had been building models too large and training them on too little data. For a compute-optimal run, parameters and training tokens should grow roughly in proportion, at about **20 tokens per parameter**. DeepMind showed this by training Chinchilla, a 70B model on about 1.4T tokens, which beat its much larger 280B predecessor Gopher at the same compute. The result pushed labs away from simply adding parameters and toward curating huge, high-quality datasets. The chat identified it as one of two forces, with [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe), behind the reversal after [GPT-4](#c/gpt-4), when frontier models got *smaller*. Chinchilla optimises training cost only. Since a model will be served many times, labs now often "over-train" smaller models well past 20 tokens per parameter.
chinchilla.article:
**Chinchilla scaling** refers to the compute-optimal scaling result published by DeepMind in 2022, named after the model trained to demonstrate it. For a fixed training-compute budget, model size and training data should be scaled together, at roughly **20 training tokens per parameter**. By that standard, the large models of the day had too many parameters and too little data.

## The finding

Training compute is roughly proportional to *parameters × tokens*, so a fixed budget can buy a bigger model trained on fewer tokens or a smaller one trained on more. Earlier scaling work had suggested putting most extra compute into parameters. The Chinchilla authors trained hundreds of models across sizes and token counts, fitted how loss depends on both, and found that the compute-optimal frontier grows parameters and tokens in roughly equal proportion.

They then tested it directly. **Chinchilla** (70B parameters, about 1.4T tokens) used the same compute as DeepMind's earlier **Gopher** (280B parameters, about 300B tokens) and outperformed it across a broad set of benchmarks. It was also 4× smaller and therefore cheaper to serve.

## Why it mattered

- **Parameters stopped being the headline.** The chat framed Chinchilla as one of two forces that "broke the parameter-equals-capability link." It "forced developers to pivot from simply building larger models to curating massive high-quality datasets," and capability that would have come from more parameters came instead from more and better data on a smaller model.
- **The size reversal.** From [GPT-1](#c/gpt-1) to [GPT-3](#c/gpt-3), parameters grew 1000× in two years, and roughly another 10× to GPT-4. Then the trend reversed in 2023. Epoch AI estimates that models like the original GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet are an order of magnitude smaller than GPT-4. (These are analyst estimates. Anthropic has never published a parameter count.)
- **Data became the bottleneck.** If a model needs about 20 tokens per parameter, trillions of high-quality tokens become necessary. That raised the importance of [web-crawl](#c/web-crawl) filtering and [data curation](#c/c-data-lever).

## Beyond the compute-optimal point

Chinchilla optimises only the *training* bill. A model that will serve billions of requests should also be cheap to run, and a smaller model is cheaper per token. So labs routinely train well past 20 tokens per parameter, accepting a less efficient training run for a smaller, cheaper-to-serve model at the same quality. Current open models are trained on tens of trillions of tokens: [Llama 4 Maverick](#c/llama4) on about 22T, and [GLM-5](#c/glm-5) on 28.5T.

[Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) complicates the ratio. Such models have separate total and active parameter counts (for example 671B total and 37B active for [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3)), so "tokens per parameter" no longer has one obvious denominator.

## Capability now rides on compute, not size

The chat's summary is that "scale" in the sense that drove about two-thirds of historical language-model gains means *training compute*, not parameter count, and the two have come apart. Frontier training compute grows about 5× per year, while parameter counts stopped tracking it. Pre-training compute efficiency improves about 3× per year, and [test-time compute](#c/reasoning-load) adds a capability axis independent of size.

## Caveats

- The 20:1 figure is an approximation from one set of fits. Later re-analyses have debated the exact coefficients, but the qualitative conclusion (scale data and parameters together) is widely accepted.
- It assumes a fixed data quality. Better data changes the curve, and [DCLM](#c/dclm) showed curation alone could match results that would otherwise need about twice the compute.

## From the chat

- The chat described Chinchilla as the 2022 finding that "for a fixed compute budget, the field had been building models too big and training them on too little data," summarised as the "Chinchilla Rule" of roughly 20 tokens per parameter.
- It named Chinchilla and MoE as the two forces behind frontier models shrinking after GPT-4, reversing the pre-2023 exponential.
- It concluded that parameter count now "tells you fairly little about where [a model] lands on a benchmark". Capability rides on training compute, data, algorithmic efficiency and test-time compute.

post-training.overview: Post-training is everything done after [pre-training](#c/pretraining) to turn a raw base model into a useful, aligned, instruction-following assistant. It uses a small fraction of total compute, yet it shapes most of the behaviour people actually interact with, including tone, refusals and personality, and since 2025 much of the reasoning ability. The classic recipe has three stages. [SFT](#c/sft) imitates curated demonstrations. [Reward modeling](#c/reward-model) learns from comparisons which response is better. Reinforcement learning ([RLHF](#c/rlhf), or [RLVR](#c/rlvr) with a checker) then optimises against that signal. [DPO](#c/dpo) folds the last two into one step. Across the stages the model moves from *imitation* toward *evaluation*, and evaluation can take it past the demonstrations it was shown. Real pipelines interleave rounds, and exact recipes are proprietary.
post-training.article:
**Post-training** is the collection of training stages applied after [pre-training](#c/pretraining) to turn a base model, a raw next-token predictor, into a helpful, instruction-following and aligned assistant. It costs a small fraction of total training compute, but it is where much of a model's observable behaviour is shaped. Two models with similar base capability can feel very different because of their post-training. The chat's summary: *pre-training builds the capabilities; post-training elicits and directs them, and adds alignment.*

## The stages

The classic recipe has three stages, and modern reasoning models add a fourth emphasis.

1. **[Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)](#c/sft).** Continue next-token prediction, but on curated prompt–response demonstrations. This teaches the basic format of being an assistant and does most of the work of converting a base model into one.
2. **[Reward modeling](#c/reward-model) / preference learning.** It is easier to *compare* two responses than to write an ideal one, so collect comparisons and train a model that scores responses.
3. **Reinforcement learning.** The model generates responses, a reward signal scores them, and the model is updated toward higher scores. [RLHF](#c/rlhf) takes its reward from a learned model of human preference. [RLVR](#c/rlvr) replaces that with a deterministic checker, which is why it dominates reasoning training in math and code. [GRPO](#c/grpo) is the algorithm that made this affordable.

[DPO](#c/dpo) is a popular lighter-weight alternative that optimises directly on preference pairs and so merges stages 2 and 3.

## The throughline: from imitation to evaluation

| Phase | What the model learns from | Ceiling |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-training | Imitating the corpus | The corpus |
| SFT | Imitating demonstrations | The demonstrations |
| RL | A judgment of quality | Can exceed the demonstrations, *if* the reward is good |

Each step relaxes a constraint, and the quality of the reward signal is "the whole ballgame." That is why swapping a noisy learned reward for a clean verifier was such a significant change.

## How much of the model changes

The standard approach is **full fine-tuning**. Every parameter can move, but with a learning rate often an order of magnitude or more below pre-training and over far fewer tokens, which avoids *catastrophic forgetting*. The alternative is parameter-efficient fine-tuning, chiefly [LoRA](#c/lora) and QLoRA. It freezes the base model and trains small adapters. It dominates outside frontier labs, while large-scale RL at the frontier generally uses full fine-tuning.

## Data

Post-training data comes in three kinds: demonstrations for SFT (often synthetic responses written by a stronger model), preference pairs (increasingly [labelled by an LLM judge](#c/llm-judge)), and [verifiable problems](#c/verifiable-problems) for RLVR. All of it gets decontaminated against benchmarks. The best public window is [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3), which released its full recipe: about 940K SFT samples and roughly 250–300K preference pairs for the 8B model. That is tiny next to pre-training, but far more expensive per example.

## Complications

- **Stages blur and repeat.** Labs interleave SFT and RL over multiple rounds, and *mid-training* sits between pre- and post-training.
- **[Distillation](#c/distillation)** is often part of the recipe. It is essentially "souped-up SFT" on a stronger model's outputs.
- **Generalist vs. specialist.** Training on many tasks brings both positive transfer and task interference. One remedy is to [specialize, then merge](#c/merging).
- **Safety and alignment** work (refusals, honesty, tone) lives mostly here.

## Why it matters now

The chat argued that recent architecture work (MLA, sparse attention, GQA and so on) has mostly bought efficiency, and that [the quality gains came from post-training](#c/c-arch-efficiency). [DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/deepseek-v32) reached GPT-5-comparable performance through "a scalable RL framework and scaled-up post-training compute," and its Speciale variant reached IMO/IOI gold-medal level.

## From the chat

- The chat framed post-training as three stages (SFT → reward model → RL), with RLHF and RLVR as two flavours of stage 3 that differ in where the reward comes from.
- The chat stressed that "the exact recipe any specific model uses … is usually proprietary". The stage structure is reliable, but specifics for any given model, Claude included, are not public.
- The chat held that the notable quality improvements of 2025 came from scaling post-training RL and test-time compute, not from architecture changes.
- On the data side, the chat said open post-training data is thinner and more dated than pre-training data. Documentation is mostly from late 2024 / early 2025, before the heavier shift to RL and agentic training.
- Agentic RL (training models to use tools over long horizons) was flagged as probably the biggest current frontier and the area where the chat was least sure of current practice.

web-crawl.overview: Filtered web crawl is the backbone of every large open pre-training corpus. C4, RefinedWeb, Dolma, RedPajama-V2, FineWeb and [DCLM](#c/dclm) all start from **Common Crawl**, a nonprofit public archive of billions of web pages collected since 2008. The raw material is enormous: DCLM offers a standardised pool of 240 trillion tokens extracted from Common Crawl. Very little of it survives. The pipeline runs [extraction and cleaning](#c/extraction), [deduplication](#c/dedup) and [model-based quality filtering](#c/quality-filter), and aggressive efforts like FineWeb-Edu and DCLM deliberately discard the lowest-quality ~90%. Curated sources are then layered on top of the filtered web text: code (GitHub), academic papers (arXiv), books, Wikipedia, Q&A sites like Stack Exchange, and math. Choosing the mixing proportions is a craft of its own. The chat noted that the filtered corpus is not a neutral window on the web. Curation choices leave measurable "fingerprints" that carry through into the trained model.

extraction.overview: Extraction and cleaning is the first refinement step for a [web-crawl](#c/web-crawl) corpus. It pulls usable text out of raw HTML and throws away the rest. Most of Common Crawl is not useful for training as it stands. The chat's examples were "three-word sentences and HTML artifacts," and navigation menus, cookie banners, boilerplate footers, spam and garbled encodings add to the pile. Extractors parse each page to isolate the main content. Heuristic filters then drop documents that fail basic checks, such as being too short, having too many symbols or repeated lines, being in the wrong language, or looking like lists of keywords. The step matters more than it seems, because the choice of extractor changes which text survives, and therefore what the model learns. It is the unglamorous start of a pipeline that continues with [deduplication](#c/dedup) and [model-based quality filtering](#c/quality-filter). Together these steps make up the data work that the chat judged [the biggest lever](#c/c-data-lever).

dedup.overview: Deduplication removes repeated content from a training corpus. The web is full of duplicates: mirrored pages, syndicated articles, templated boilerplate, near-identical copies differing by a date or an ad. Training on the same text many times wastes compute and can hurt quality. It over-weights whatever happens to be copied, and it encourages memorisation over generalisation. Modern pipelines deduplicate at several granularities. **Document-level** dedup drops exact copies. **Paragraph-** or line-level dedup removes repeated blocks inside otherwise distinct pages; [DCLM](#c/dclm)-Baseline does this "to increase novelty and reduce redundancy." **Fuzzy** dedup catches near-duplicates, typically with hashing schemes such as MinHash that estimate overlap without comparing every pair. Deduplication follows [extraction](#c/extraction) and sits alongside [quality filtering](#c/quality-filter). It is related to, but separate from, [decontamination](#c/decontamination), which specifically removes overlap with evaluation benchmarks.

quality-filter.overview: Model-based quality filtering is where the chat located "the real leverage" in pre-training data. Rule-based heuristics give way to a small learned classifier that scores every document for quality, and only the top slice is kept. [DCLM](#c/dclm)'s recipe trains a fastText classifier with instruction-formatted data and high-quality r/ExplainLikeImFive posts as positive examples, ranks the whole crawl, and **keeps only the top ~10%**. FineWeb-Edu similarly discards about 90%. The payoff is large. DCLM-Baseline let a 7B model reach 64% MMLU on only 2.6T tokens, and beat the prior open-data state of the art by about 6 MMLU points at *half the compute*. That is curation buying what would otherwise take twice the compute. The catch is that the definition of "good" is a consequential design decision, and filtered datasets carry measurable fingerprints into the trained model. See [data curation is the biggest lever](#c/c-data-lever).

decontamination.overview: Decontamination removes training examples that overlap with the benchmarks a model will be evaluated on. Without it, a high score may mean the model has *seen the test*, not that it can solve it. Leakage is easy. Benchmark questions get posted, discussed and copied across the web, and they reach pre-training crawls. [Post-training](#c/post-training) datasets, often assembled from public sources or synthesised by models that saw those benchmarks, are especially prone to it. The usual method checks for n-gram or near-duplicate overlap between training data and benchmark test sets, and drops or rewrites the matches. [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3) made "strict decontamination" a central step: it surveyed available datasets, analysed their provenance, and decontaminated them. [Verifiable-problem](#c/verifiable-problems) datasets for RLVR likewise pair careful difficulty balancing with benchmark-leakage removal. The chat called decontamination "a recurring obsession" and the post-training counterpart of the quality problem. Since most labs never disclose their data, outside observers cannot fully check it for closed models.

synthetic-sft.overview: Synthetic SFT responses are training demonstrations written by a strong model rather than by people. [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3), Ai2's fully open post-training recipe, stated plainly that *all* of its new synthetic SFT datasets had responses generated by GPT-4o, or by Claude 3.5 Sonnet for coding, because those gave the highest quality. Regenerating completions for existing datasets through this pipeline even improved downstream [DPO](#c/dpo) results. This is output-based [distillation](#c/distillation). With a closed teacher you cannot see its weights or probabilities, so you train on what it writes. It is cheap and it works. Alpaca, Open Orca and TinyGSM (12.3M synthetic problems that took a 125M model to 63.1% on grade-school math) are the classic cases. The chat's point was that even the flagship *open* post-training effort depends on closed frontier models for its targets. Closed labs cannot do this for their own frontier models, so they rely more on human experts.

llm-judge.overview: LLM-as-a-judge means using a language model, rather than a human annotator, to decide which of two responses is better. It has become the backbone of open preference-data pipelines. [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3) documents a three-stage process. It selects prompts, generates responses from a pool of models (including the model being trained, to get on-policy data), and has an LLM judge rate them to form (preferred, rejected) pairs for [reward modeling](#c/reward-model) or [DPO](#c/dpo). The draw is scale. Model judgments are cheap and fast compared with paid annotators, so pipelines can cover far more prompts. Humans have not vanished, though. Qwen2 describes a hybrid of human annotation and automated synthesis, with people concentrated where judgment is hardest. The chat flagged the open question: LLM judges have their own biases and failure modes. Their reliability is now "load-bearing for the whole preference-data pipeline," and how much human judgment remains in frontier preference data is undisclosed.

verifiable-problems.overview: Verifiable problems are the training data for [RLVR](#c/rlvr): tasks whose answers a program can check. Examples are math problems with known solutions, coding tasks with unit tests, and instructions with programmatically checkable constraints ("answer in exactly three bullet points"). Instead of demonstrations or preference pairs, the dataset is *problems plus verification machinery*. The model attempts each problem, the checker returns pass/fail, and [GRPO](#c/grpo)-style RL reinforces the attempts that pass. [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3)'s final stage selected tasks with verifiable outcomes and gave reward only when a generation was verified correct. The chat called this data "smallest but highest-leverage". Curation matters: good sets are balanced toward medium difficulty, since problems that are always solved or never solved give no gradient. They are [decontaminated](#c/decontamination) and often ordered into a curriculum. The limiting factor is *having a verifier*, which is why RLVR stays concentrated in math, code and format-following.
